topic.title: Fans grade players like an appraisal
topic.claim: We judge Rohit and Kohli the way offices judge people: the last bad quarter erases the record.
topic.behaviour: Three ducks in one innings and the timeline wants them retired. Two days later India win the series and the mood changes without anyone admitting it was an overreaction.
topic.mechanism: Online anger is cheap and instant, and it gets rewarded with replies. The latest result is the only data point that feels real, so it counts for everything.
topic.group: Cricket fans and office workers, 24 to 32
topic.moment: You type 'should have retired' at 9 pm and quietly change your mind by Sunday.

turn.believed: We judge players on their whole career.
turn.actually: We judge them on the last match, the same way an appraisal judges you on the last quarter.

topic.villain: A feed that rewards the loudest reaction to the latest result
topic.because: Outrage gets engagement, and engagement is what the platforms and channels sell. Nobody earns anything from saying 'wait and see'.

proof.fact: India were 0/3 after the first over, with Rohit Sharma out on the first ball, Virat Kohli bowled for a four-ball duck and Shreyas Iyer out on the last ball. Fans said Rohit and Kohli should have retired three years ago, while many others still want the pair at the 2027 ODI World Cup.

topic.payoff: Test: would you give your own career the verdict you just gave Kohli on a bad day?
topic.send_to: The group-chat friend who declares a player finished after one bad innings.
real_details: India won the fifth ODI by 22 runs to take the series 3-1, two days after the collapse in the fourth
topic.news_peg: India's top-order ducks in the 4th ODI on 2026-11-13 and the series win on 2026-11-15
topic.why_now: The whole swing from outrage to relief happened inside two days.

cover.headline: We judge Rohit and Kohli like an [appraisal judges you]
cover.sub: One bad first over, and a whole career gets voted out.

paragraphs:
We judge Rohit and Kohli like offices judge us. The last bad quarter erases the whole record.
Swipe →
slides.why_swipe: What bad quarter? Which match is this about?

paragraphs: Take last week's fourth ODI against New Zealand. In the very first over, Rohit went first ball and Kohli was bowled for a duck.
Within minutes, every WhatsApp group in the country became a selection committee.
The verdict: "Should have retired three years ago."
Two days later India won the series, and the same timeline that wanted them gone moved on like nothing had happened.
You didn't go back and delete your message either.
slides.why_swipe: Was one bad over the whole story?

paragraphs: Your message also skipped the first match of the same series. Kohli made 74 in it.
slides.why_swipe: So was the anger wrong, or just loud?

paragraphs: To be fair, the worry isn't made up. Apart from that 74, both barely scored, and questions lingered after the win.
But "his form worries me" and "get him out" are different sentences. Only one of them gets replies.
slides.why_swipe: Why does the louder one win?

paragraphs: And replies are the whole business. "Let's wait and see" gets two likes. "Coward, drop them" gets a reaction video with a red arrow on the thumbnail.
Within the hour, some highlights channel asks "END OF AN ERA?" Nobody makes money from patience.
slides.why_swipe: Where else does this same rule show up?

paragraphs: The rule is simple: your last score is your only score.
Which is funny, because you hate this rule at work. Eleven solid months, one messy March, and the appraisal remembers March.
Then you run it on Kohli after every match.
slides.why_swipe: When does that rule suddenly feel unfair?

paragraphs: Until your manager pings "quick call tomorrow?" at 9 pm. Suddenly you want all twelve months counted.
You want the full record you wouldn't give Kohli for one over.

end.save: Read it again before you type "should retire" after the next collapse.

draft.alt_text: A ten-slide text post. In the fourth ODI against New Zealand, India were 0 for 3 in the first over, with Rohit Sharma out first ball and Virat Kohli bowled for a duck, and group chats acted like selection committees, calling for them to retire. Two days later India won the series, and Kohli's 74 at the start of the same series had already been forgotten. The post says worries about form are fair, but the feed rewards outrage, like reaction videos and 'end of an era' thumbnails, over patience, because replies are the business. It argues your last score becomes your only score, the same way an appraisal judges us on the latest result, even though we hate that rule at work. It ends with the late-night message from your manager, when you suddenly want your whole year counted, the full record you wouldn't give Kohli.
